clinicalPearls: An epithelium-lined outpouching arising from the urethra, most commonly in women along the mid or distal posterior urethra
The classic triad (the 'three Ds') is dysuria, dyspareunia, and post-void dribbling, though presentations vary widely
A tender anterior vaginal wall mass that may express pus or urine from the meatus on compression is characteristic
Symptoms are often chronic and non-specific, so diagnosis is frequently delayed and the condition is mistaken for recurrent cystitis or vaginitis
MRI of the pelvis and urethra is the most sensitive imaging test and best defines the anatomy; voiding cystourethrography, ultrasound, and urethroscopy also contribute
Management is surgical excision (diverticulectomy) with urethral reconstruction for symptomatic cases, while small asymptomatic diverticula may be observed
Complications include recurrent infection, stone formation within the diverticulum, and, rarely, malignancy arising in the diverticular lining
reference.pathophysiology: Most acquired female urethral diverticula are thought to arise from the periurethral (paraurethral or Skene's) glands. Repeated infection and obstruction of these glands lead to abscess formation, which then ruptures into the urethral lumen and leaves an epithelium-lined cavity communicating with the urethra through a neck. Urine and debris collect in this sac and drain intermittently, producing post-void dribbling and recurrent infection, while stasis predisposes to stone formation and, rarely, malignant change. The size and location of the sac and its ostium determine the clinical picture and the surgical approach.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent urinary tract infection or cystitis
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the urethra and pelvis
Double-balloon positive-pressure urethrography where MRI is unavailable
redFlags: A firm or fixed mass or a solid component suggesting malignancy within the diverticulum
A stone within the diverticulum with severe pain
reference.prognosis: Good after complete surgical excision, with most patients gaining symptom relief; recurrence, urethrovaginal fistula, or stress incontinence can complicate surgery, and rare diverticular malignancy worsens the outlook.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating 'recurrent cystitis' without considering a diverticulum as the underlying cause
Relying on examination alone and not obtaining dedicated MRI to define the anatomy
Missing a malignancy or a stone arising within the diverticulum
Incomplete excision leaving a residual sac and causing recurrence or fistula
